title: Seeing with sound
text: Shout into a canyon and the echo comes back; a bat has simply turned that accident into a {{1}}. By emitting ultrasonic calls far above our hearing and measuring how long the {{2}} takes to return, it builds a sound picture of the world accurate enough to catch a moth in mid-air, in total darkness. The details are astonishing. Some bats can detect a wire thinner than a {{3}} of hair; others adjust the loudness of every call to keep the returning echo constant, a feat of automatic {{4}} control that engineers later copied for radar. Moths, in turn, have developed {{5}} of their own: some hear the bat's approach and dive away, while one tropical species answers with clicks that {{6}} the bat's sonar, jamming it like static on a radio. Bats are not alone. Dolphins echolocate underwater with clicks focused through a fatty {{7}} in the forehead, and some blind people have learned a version of the same trick, clicking their tongues and reading the echoes off nearby walls, then {{8}} their way around unfamiliar streets in perfect safety. Where light fails, evolution keeps finding a way to listen instead.

gaps.explanation: 'turned the accident into a system' — a working method; symptom = sign of illness, syllable = unit of sound.
'how long the echo takes to return' — the reflected sound; the context of sound rules out image, odour and orbit.
'a strand of hair' — one thin thread; 'a string of' collocates with pearls or words, and strap, stripe and stump do not fit at all.
'a feat of automatic volume control' — loudness; pitch and tone are other sound parameters, and tempo belongs to music.
'have developed defences of their own' — protective countermeasures; defeat = loss, defect = fault, deficit = shortfall.
'clicks that jam the bat's sonar' — interfere with it deliberately; jar means grate on, and the passage compares the effect to radio static.
'a fatty organ in the forehead' — a specialised body part; instruments, devices and utensils are made objects.
'feeling their way around unfamiliar streets' — moving carefully by touch or trial; the fixed idiom needs 'feeling', not the near-forms.
